title: Acerta — Hosted Gen sandbox playthrough: real-time basics + failure mitigation
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation focused on streaming behavior, key parameters, retry and idempotency patterns, and console knobs to control cost/latency. Customer wants to validate low-latency path for payments assistant and ask about VPC/private options and SOC2/KMS. Agreed to run a small benchmark and share security package.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Location: Zoom / Redwood sandbox environment
Link references: console.redwood.ai/sandbox (demo), /docs/security/soc2.pdf (sent afterwards)

[00:00:00] Laura (AE): All right everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Laura from Redwood Inference, I'm here with Marcus and Diego. How are you all?
[00:00:06] Priya (Acerta): Hey hi, good thanks. Sofia and Tom are here too. Thanks for setting this up — we wanted a quick walkthrough of hosted realtime gen and to see how retries look under our sample traffic.
[00:00:18] Laura: Great, we'll hit streaming first — the low-latency path — and then show the console metrics and retry patterns. Marcus will do the live sandpit.
[00:00:26] Marcus (SE): Cool. Quick intro — we assume you're using the Hosted API with an API key. For realtime chat we stream tokens back over an event stream so you get first-token latency often < 100ms for short prompts on our small models and ~200-400ms on larger ones depending on sequence length and batching.
[00:00:45] Tom (Acerta): When you say batching does that mean the service holds requests to batch them and that adds latency? We care about single-user latency for the payments assistant.
[00:00:53] Marcus: Good question. We have adaptive batching — it only batches when throughput suggests it benefits cost. For strict single-user low-latency you can set the policy to minimal batching or use the fastpath model family. We'll show the console knob for that.
[00:01:06] [00:01:06] Marcus: I'll switch to the sandbox — share screen — and run a sample chat. Note: transcript audio's a bit fuzzy, apologies if some product names sound off.
[00:01:16] [00:01:16] Marcus (screen share): Here's the request — prompt is our payments assistant starter, temperature 0.0, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 128, stream=true. We add a request_id header to correlate logs for idempotency.
[00:01:30] Sofia: Can you explain the request_id pattern? We have problems with duplicate messages when mobile clients retry.
[00:01:34] Marcus: Yes. We recommend client-generated idempotency keys: attach x-request-id and set idempotency=true on the endpoint. If the request with that id is retried, we dedupe on the server side and return the original response or a fallback. This prevents double charges or double sends.
[00:01:49] Priya: Nice. Does that persist across model variants? E.g., if a fallback model is used because the preferred model is overloaded, will the same idempotency key get the same content?
[00:01:58] Marcus: We try to keep deterministic behavior but smaller/fallback models can diverge. Our default policy is: if the original request completed and was recorded against the id, we return the recorded output. If the original failed mid-generation, and a retry hits a different model, you'll get the new generation. You can configure strict-mode to force fallback to stored cached completions where applicable.
[00:02:19] [00:02:19] Diego: Also worth noting our prefix/KV cache, which can make retries much cheaper for repeated prompts with similar prefixes — it's on by default for Hosted API.
[00:02:26] Tom: Ok cool. Can you show a failure — like an interrupted stream — and how the client should reconnect?
[00:02:31] Marcus: Sure. I'm going to simulate a dropped connection on the stream.
[00:02:35] [00:02:35] Marcus: (types) ... simulating network drop.
[00:02:39] [00:02:39] Speaker 1: (laugh) nice.
[00:02:41] Marcus: On the client we recommend a short exponential backoff and to include the same request_id. For streaming we also support resume tokens for partial transcripts — so the client can request continuation from the last successful token offset. It's not perfect for all models but it reduces re-gen.
[00:02:55] Priya: Resume tokens — are those in the SDK already or do we need to handle offsets?
[00:02:59] Marcus: SDK includes helpers in our JS/Go SDKs. The raw API supports last_token_index in the resume request. SDK will patch headers for you.
[00:03:07] [00:03:07] Sofia: We heard about continuous batching and about the KV cache — how do these impact deterministic outputs for compliance logs? We need to store exact outputs for audits.
[00:03:15] Marcus: Good point. The console gives you complete per-request transcripts and a token-level log you can export. If you enable audit retention > 90 days (enterprise add-on) we persist the generation artifacts and the model version used so you can replay. Batching is transparent at the visible API level — you still get the full recorded output per request.
[00:03:33] Tom: And encryption at rest? KMS?
[00:03:35] Laura: We support customer-managed keys (AWS KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we offer KMS integration for audit logs and encryption of exported artifacts — we'll attach the security doc.
[00:03:48] [00:03:48] Marcus: Back to retries: we recommend the following client strategy — short retry budget, exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency keys, and when in doubt, a single full-request retry rather than lots of small retries to avoid double billing. We'll demo a backoff script.
[00:04:05] [00:04:05] Marcus (screen): Running a small synthetic where we fire 50 requests at once with 3 concurrent clients to emulate bursts. Watch the stream behaviour.
[00:04:13] [00:04:13] (UI noise)
[00:04:16] Marcus: You can see in the console metrics that some requests go through the fastpath and some were batched for a micro-batch window. The latency distribution slides to the right for batched requests but cost per token drops.
[00:04:30] Priya: What's the micro-batch window? 10ms? 50ms?
[00:04:33] Marcus: Default is adaptive; typically 5-20 ms depending on model and current qps. You can set a strict low-latency policy which effectively disables batching at the expense of cost.
[00:04:45] Sofia: For payments assistant we want 95p latency < 300ms for 40-token replies. Is that feasible?
[00:04:51] Marcus: Yes, on the fastpath family with minimal batching and a small prompt and temperature 0 we generally hit that. We'll need the exact prompts to bench — that's the benchmark step.
[00:04:59] [00:04:59] Priya: Can you walk us through parameter tuning? We want concise replies, very deterministic.
[00:05:06] Marcus: Sure — temperature 0 for deterministic, often combined with top_p 0.9 or 0.95. Use max_tokens to bound length; use stop sequences to cut off. Also use presence_penalty/ frequency_penalty to manage repetition — though for short assistant answers not always necessary.
[00:05:22] Tom: Any tricks for token cost reduction without hurting latency?
[00:05:25] Marcus: You can enable prefix caching for repeated boilerplate — that keeps KV cache across requests. Also use a smaller instruct-tuned model for routine tasks and route to larger model only for edge cases. The Console has routing policies to do canary rollouts between model variants.
[00:05:38] [00:05:38] Diego: We also showed Optimize earlier — and optimize will suggest quantization profiles and batch sizes based on your prompt distribution to hit cost targets while keeping latency SLOs. We'll attach that Optimize report template for your team to fill.
[00:05:51] Sofia: Great. For retries, is there a token-level billing transparency? If a stream partially completes and then is retried, how are we billed?
[00:05:59] Marcus: Billing is per-token generated. If a partial stream was returned and you retry, the tokens from the failed attempt may be charged; we provide detailed token logs so you can analyze wasted token cost and set a retry policy. In some cases we offer intelligent retry suppression if the partial output was adequate.
[00:06:16] Priya: Hmm, so we need to watch for our mobile clients frequently retrying and causing double tokens. We'll need guidance.
[00:06:21] Laura: We'll include best-practice client patterns in the shared doc — e.g., debounce on mobile, detect transient errors vs server errors, and prefer idempotency keys.
[00:06:29] [00:06:29] Marcus (screen): Now I'll show a controlled error mode — we limit capacity and cause a 503 for one model, watch the fallback routing.
[00:06:36] [00:06:36] (screen)
[00:06:40] Marcus: The console shows an automatic fallback to a compatible model family; in the request logs you can see the route decision and the reason code. We also annotate when caching or prior completions were used.
[00:06:52] Tom: If the fallback model returns slightly different content, how do we surface that to the app?
[00:06:56] Marcus: We add response metadata: model_version, route_reason, and a compatibility_score. The client can choose to surface a QA check or escalate to human review if the compatibility_score is low.
[00:07:07] Sofia: That compatibility_score — is that deterministic? It's internal heuristic?
[00:07:10] Marcus: It's a heuristic based on token overlap and semantic similarity; not a perfect guarantee but useful for routing UI decisions.
[00:07:17] [00:07:17] Priya: Let's talk about console and tracing. We need to be able to match a user transaction to an API call — correlation IDs etc.
[00:07:23] Marcus: Put your correlation id in x-correlation-id header. Console tracing shows per-request timeline — request received, queued, model started, token stream. You can export spans to Jaeger/Datadog.
[00:07:35] Tom: Good, that's important. For compliance, we need full audit logs and retention. You mentioned an enterprise add-on — what's the cost model?
[00:07:42] Laura: We'll include pricing tiers in the packet, but generally audit retention and longer logs are an add-on priced monthly; Dedicated and Private include different retention options in contract.
[00:07:51] [00:07:51] Sofia: Any red flags we should know about for production on Hosted? Data residency?
[00:07:55] Laura: Hosted has region support — EU/US/APAC. For strict data residency or air-gapped, Private deployment or Dedicated in your VPC is the right path. We'll map cost and onboarding timelines (Private takes longer due to network setup).
[00:08:08] Priya: Onboarding timeline — we need something in production in Q2, is that realistic?
[00:08:12] Laura: For Hosted yes. For Dedicated possibly if you sign a committed capacity agreement soon. Private is multi-quarter typically.
[00:08:20] [00:08:20] Marcus: Back to practical debugging — here's a sample of a streaming transcript with a reconnect and resume token.
[00:08:26] (screen shows JSON snippet)
[00:08:29] Marcus: Notice the token offsets and the resume_token field. If you replay with the same request_id and resume_token we continue. If a different model is used on retry it's best-effort.
[00:08:40] Priya: Understood. We also want to test bursty loads as during statement generation spikes. The payments flow will generate many small replies. Is there an autoscale lag?
[00:08:49] Marcus: Our Hosted pool autoscaling operates in sub-minute ranges for typical traffic and the Dedicated pool has reserved capacity you control. There's a cold-start behavior if you spin a new model variant — we give warmup guidelines in the docs.
[00:09:01] Tom: What about rate-limits and quotas? We might want to throttle per-user.
[00:09:05] Marcus: You can implement per-token and per-route rate-limits via the Console. For Hosted we also enforce per-account quotas; for enterprise we can expose per-API-key quotas and token buckets.
[00:09:16] [00:09:16] Sofia: Any gotchas around stop sequences and streaming? Sometimes stop tokens don't flush properly and we see trailing partial words.
[00:09:22] Marcus: For streaming the SDK will buffer until a stop is emitted or the token finishes; clients should handle partial token flushes and use the final event type (e.g., [DONE]) to know a generation is complete. There's edge behavior for certain tokenizers where partial bytes look like characters — SDKs help smooth that.
[00:09:38] Priya: Ok good. Could you share a recommended client pseudo-code pattern for streaming + retries?
[00:09:42] Marcus: Sure — we'll put it in the shared repo, but quick: generate request_id, open stream, on network error do exponential backoff, if you have resume_token request resume, if you receive partial and it's acceptable mark complete and don't retry, otherwise issue a single full retry.
[00:09:58] [00:09:58] Priya: That helps. One more question — our product team cares about hallucinations. Any built-in mitigations?
[00:10:04] Diego: You can do grounding via tool-calling patterns or retrieval augmented generation. Redwood supports calling out to a retrieval system (RAG) and we provide structured tool-call framing so the model is given citations. We also surface score/confidence heuristics.
[00:10:18] Sofia: Are tool calls supported in streaming?
[00:10:20] Marcus: Yes — we stream partial tokens until tool call is triggered, then send a tool-call event and stream the tool result back; it's a bit more complex but supported.
[00:10:29] [00:10:29] Laura: Ok pulling back — let's recap next steps and who owns what.
[00:10:33] Priya: We'll provide the 3 golden prompts and a target 95p latency.
[00:10:37] Tom: We'll also share our current traffic shape and a sample mobile client retry pattern.
[00:10:41] Marcus: We'll prepare the load script and share instructions.
[00:10:44] Laura: I'll send the security pack (SOC2, encryption options, vendor questionnaire) and an initial Hosted vs Dedicated cost outline.
[00:10:51] Sofia: Sounds good. Can we also get a one-page summary for our execs focusing on risk & mitigation?
[00:10:56] Laura: Yes — we'll produce a 1-pager with SLO fit, compliance notes, and suggested rollout.
[00:11:02] [00:11:02] Priya: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:05] (meeting winds down — brief cross chatter)

[00:11:20] End notes: Attendees agreed to a follow-up benchmark the week of 2025-03-17. Marcus will provide the scripts and Laura will attach the security docs. The console links and sample payloads will be emailed.
